summary: This RFC specifies how to wrap IP datagrams for sending over an Experimental Ethernet, an early form of Ethernet. It gives the basic framing so that IP hosts on the same cable can exchange packets.

plainLanguage.summary: This explains how to put Internet letters into the right envelope so they can travel along the early Ethernet cable.

questions: how to send ip over experimental ethernet
how are ip datagrams sent over experimental ethernet
what is the experimental ethernet type field value
what is the experimental ethernet maximum datagram size
subtitle: How IP datagrams ride inside frames on the 3-megabit Experimental Ethernet.

tldr.problem: IP hosts on an Experimental Ethernet need a standard way to put IP datagrams into Ethernet frames.
tldr.mechanism: The frame's type field holds 513 (1001 octal) and the data field holds the IP header and data, padded if needed. Hosts use the last eight bits of the IP host number as their 8-bit Ethernet address.
tldr.outcome: The RFC is an Internet Standard for the Experimental Ethernet (3-megabit/second, 8-bit addresses). The 10-megabit, 48-bit Ethernet is covered separately by RFC 894.

today: RFC 895 is an Internet Standard and has not been obsoleted or updated. It covers only the Experimental Ethernet; the 10-megabit Ethernet is covered by RFC 894.

sections.title: Scope: The Experimental Ethernet
sections.content: RFC 895 specifies a standard method of encapsulating Internet Protocol (IP) datagrams on an Experimental Ethernet, which runs at 3 megabits per second and uses 8-bit addresses. Sending IP datagrams on the 10-megabit, 48-bit address Ethernet is described separately in RFC 894.
sections.plainLanguage: This is the rulebook for sending Internet letters over the very first, slower Ethernet cable.

sections.title: Frame Format and Size
sections.content:
IP datagrams travel in standard Experimental Ethernet frames. The frame's type field must contain 513 (1001 octal), and the data field holds the IP header followed immediately by the IP data. If needed, the data field should be padded to meet the minimum frame size; the padding is not part of the IP packet and is not counted in the IP total length field.

The maximum length of an IP datagram on this network is 1536 octets. Implementations are encouraged to support full-length packets, and gateways MUST accept them and fragment them if necessary. A system that cannot receive full-length packets should discourage others from sending them, for example with the TCP Maximum Segment Size option (RFC 879).

Datagrams on the Ethernet may be longer than the general Internet default maximum of 576 octets, so hosts sending to machines on other networks may want smaller datagrams to avoid fragmentation at gateways.
sections.plainLanguage: Each frame is an envelope stamped with a special number, 513, so receivers know an Internet letter is inside. If the letter is too small, padding fills the envelope.

sections.title: Address Mapping and Broadcast
sections.content:
Mapping a 32-bit Internet address to an 8-bit Experimental Ethernet address can be done several ways. The easiest, and the recommended approach, is to use the last eight bits of the host number part of the Internet address as the host's Ethernet address.

The broadcast Internet address (the host part is all binary ones) should be mapped to the broadcast Experimental Ethernet address, which is address zero.
sections.plainLanguage: Each computer's short street number is just the last part of its Internet address. Shouting to everyone uses the special number zero.

sections.title: Trailers and Byte Order
sections.content:
Some versions of Unix 4.2bsd use a different encapsulation, called trailers, for better performance on the VAX. Consenting systems on the same Ethernet may use it between themselves, but no host is required to implement it, and trailer-format datagrams should be sent only when the sender knows the recipient can interpret them. Details are in RFC 893.

The IP datagram is sent over the Ethernet as a series of 8-bit bytes, as described in Appendix B of the Internet Protocol specification (RFC 791).
sections.plainLanguage: Some machines use a different way of packing the envelope. It is optional, and you should only use it with machines you know understand it.
